result:
It’s strange how a number can sit in your head like a quiet appointment. 1000 words. Not 500, not 2000. A thousand. It’s enough to build a small room in, enough to get lost in, enough that you can’t just dash it off on impulse and you can’t pretend it’s a big deal either. It’s a polite, reasonable demand.

I keep thinking about the kitchen at 7:13 a.m. The kettle is humming and the light is that thin, winter kind that makes everything look a little washed out. My phone is on the counter with a notification I haven’t opened. There’s a mug with a chip on the rim that I keep meaning to throw away. I should be making coffee. Instead I am here, trying to fill a thousand words with whatever comes to you, which is a trick question because whatever comes to you is always the same few things recycled in different weather.

First comes the to-do list. The dishes from last night. The email to Maya about the invoice. The plant that needs repotting. The thought that I haven’t called my father in three weeks. The list is long and it is always first because the mind likes to file everything under unfinished business before it lets you do anything unproductive.

Then comes the body. My left shoulder is tight. I can feel it pulling down toward my ear. I have been sitting too long. I should stretch. The chair is not comfortable. The floor is cold under my socks. There is a faint smell of laundry detergent from the load I put in yesterday. My stomach is a little empty. I could eat toast. I could drink water.

Then comes the story. Or the half-story. About the time I got lost in the train station in Prague and ended up buying a ticket to a town I’d never heard of because the ticket machine only took coins and I had too many coins. I rode three stops and got off because I was tired of being lost. The town was quiet. There were geese on a canal. A man was fixing a bicycle in the rain. I sat on a bench and read a paperback I’d brought for the journey but never opened. That is a story that wants to be told but it never gets told properly because it doesn’t have a moral.

Maybe the point is that there is no point. You were told to write whatever comes to you and so whatever comes is what you have to work with. It’s a kind of permission slip. Most days we are too careful. We edit the first sentence before we even finish it. We ask: is this interesting? Is this correct? Is this the right tone? But here the instruction is to bypass all that. Just let the words come.

Sometimes the words come fast. Sometimes they come in clumps. A memory, a fragment of a song, a question you didn’t ask out loud. I can hear the neighbor’s dog barking at intervals. The kettle clicks off. The light moves a few inches across the table. Time does that.

I think about how writing is mostly listening. Not to some grand voice but to the small chatter underneath. The part of you that notices the way the chip in the mug catches the light. The part that wonders if anyone else is awake in this building. The part that is secretly afraid of running out of things to say, which is a fear every writer has, and a fear every person has when they sit down to be honest.

If I had to pick one image to carry through these thousand words it would be the window. It’s not a dramatic window. It’s a normal kitchen window with a little grime in the corner and a sticker from the realtor left on the glass from when we moved in. Outside is the street, a parked car, a tree that is mostly bare. The window frames the world and also limits it. You see a slice and you imagine the rest.

Words are like that. You put down a slice and hope the reader imagines the rest. You can’t describe everything. You can’t even describe yourself completely. There is always a back room you never clean out. A drawer of old receipts. A box of photographs with no names on the back.

I wonder who will read this. Probably no one. Maybe you. Maybe the system. Maybe I’m just writing to prove I can fill the space. That’s a valid reason too. We fill spaces. We fill silence. We fill the pause between one thought and the next with words because the alternative is to sit with the quiet and hear how loud it can be.

The shoulder is still tight. I should roll it. The coffee would be good now. The list is still there. Maya. The plant. My father. The invoice. They will wait. They always wait.

There is a kind of freedom in not having to be good. When the requirement is just to write, you can be messy. You can contradict yourself three sentences in a row. You can start a paragraph with “I think” and end it with “I don’t know.” You can admit that you are making this up as you go, which you are.

I keep coming back to the number. 1000. It’s a round number. It feels complete. It’s the number of pages in some books, the number of hours in about 41 days, the number of steps to a mile if you are walking fast. It’s not infinite, which is comforting. You can finish.

Maybe that’s what we want most days: an ending we can see. A container that will hold us for a while. A thousand words is a container. You can put things in it. You can put the kettle and the mug and the chipped rim and the geese on the canal and the man fixing the bicycle and the tight shoulder and the fear of running out. You can put all of it in and still have room for a little more.

The light has moved again. The street outside is a little brighter. Someone is walking a dog. The dog is pulling. The person is trying to keep it steady. That’s a small drama, repeated everywhere.

I think I’m close. Not to the end, exactly, but to the feeling of having said enough for now. The words have been coming in waves. First the practical, then the sensory, then the reflective, then the tired. That’s the order they usually come in when I sit down without a plan.

If you were told to write whatever comes to you, you would probably start with what is nearest. The room. The body. The list. Then you would wander. That’s fine. Wandering is the point. If you stay still you only get one sentence.

So I’ll keep going until the count feels right. I’ll let the sentences run a little long, then cut them short. I’ll let the thoughts overlap. I’ll admit I don’t know why I am writing this, except because I was asked to. And because there is a pleasure in watching the page fill, in seeing the white space shrink, in knowing that for a few minutes I was paying attention.

There is a final cup of coffee waiting. The plant needs water. The phone is still lit. The world is still out there beyond the window. And I have a thousand words to give it, or to give myself, or to give you. Whatever comes is enough.
